zfbehavior analyzes zebrafish larval light-dark transition test (LDTT)
data and developmental toxicity, from the vendor's tracking files to hit
calls and benchmark concentrations (BMC). It comes with **Agent Skills**:
step-by-step guides that a coding agent (or a person) follows to run one
analysis step, ask you for every scientific choice, and render a report.
This vignette explains how to use them. The methods behind each step are in
`vignette("methods", package = "zfbehavior")`.

## Modules and skills

The workflow has five modules. A module is a method step; a skill is what
you run. Each skill run gets its own folder with a report and outputs.

| # | Module | Skills |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Data import and consistency checks | `dataset-import-qc` |
| 2 | Raw-response visualization and inter-plate VC QC | `raw-response-plots`, `interplate-vc-qc` |
| 3 | Endpoint calculation, normalization, and intra-plate VC QC | `behavior-endpoints`, `intraplate-vc-qc`, `devtox-endpoints` |
| 4 | ANOVA/repeated-measures ANOVA hit calling | `behavior-endpoints-anova` |
| 5 | Curvep-based BMC modeling of behavioral and developmental toxicity endpoints | `behavior-endpoints-bmc`, `devtox-endpoints-bmc` |

A skill reads the outputs of the skills before it (VC = vehicle control;
`[QC]` runs are optional and only list plates to exclude):

```text
dataset-import-qc  (M1)
 |-- raw-response-plots  (M2)
 |-- [QC] interplate-vc-qc  (M2)
 |-- behavior-endpoints  (M3)
 |    |-- [QC] intraplate-vc-qc  (M3)
 |    |-- behavior-endpoints-anova  (M4)
 |    `-- behavior-endpoints-bmc  (M5)
 `-- devtox-endpoints  (M3)
      `-- devtox-endpoints-bmc  (M5)
```

A usual behavior run: `dataset-import-qc` -> `raw-response-plots` ->
`interplate-vc-qc` -> `behavior-endpoints` -> `intraplate-vc-qc` ->
`behavior-endpoints-anova` and/or `behavior-endpoints-bmc`. The
developmental toxicity branch is `devtox-endpoints` ->
`devtox-endpoints-bmc`.

## Setup

You need R (>= 4.1), [Quarto](https://quarto.org) (the skills render
Quarto reports), and the package with its dependencies, including Rcurvep:

```{r}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("moggces/zfbehavior")
```

The skills are installed with the package. Find them with:

```{r}
system.file("skills", package = "zfbehavior")
#> .../zfbehavior/skills
#>   CONVENTIONS.md
#>   dataset-import-qc/SKILL.md, templates/
#>   raw-response-plots/SKILL.md, templates/
#>   ...
```

Each skill folder has a `SKILL.md` (the guide) and `templates/` (a Quarto
report `.qmd` and its parameter file `.yml`). `CONVENTIONS.md` holds the
rules shared by all skills.

## Giving the skills to an agent

Any coding agent that can read files and run a shell can use the skills.
Two ways:

1. **Point the agent at the file.** In your prompt, give the path of the
   `SKILL.md`, e.g. "Read
   `<path from system.file()>/dataset-import-qc/SKILL.md` and
   `CONVENTIONS.md` next to it, then import the data in `data/raw/`."
2. **Install them as agent skills.** Agents that support the Agent Skills
   format find skills in a fixed folder, e.g.
   `~/.config/opencode/skills/` (opencode) or `.claude/skills/` in your
   project (Claude Code). Copy or link the skill folders there:

   ```{bash}
   SKILLS=$(Rscript -e 'cat(system.file("skills", package = "zfbehavior"))')
   mkdir -p ~/.config/opencode/skills
   ln -s "$SKILLS" ~/.config/opencode/skills/zfbehavior
   ```

   A link follows package updates; a copy does not. The agent then picks a
   skill by its description when you ask, e.g., "import the new zebrafish
   batch".

The skills call only exported zfbehavior functions, and render with the
**installed** package, so update the package before re-running a skill
after an update.

## Project layout

All results go into your analysis project, never into the package:

```text
my-project/
|-- data/raw/260416/                       vendor files, never modified
`-- analysis/
    |-- dataset-import-qc/260416/          one folder per run
    |   |-- dataset-import-qc.qmd            copied template
    |   |-- dataset-import-qc.yml            your choices, with reasons
    |   |-- dataset-import-qc.html           report
    |   `-- outputs/
    |       |-- dataset-import-qc__260416__combined.rds
    |       `-- dataset-import-qc__260416__manifest.yml
    `-- behavior-endpoints/260416/
        `-- behavior-endpoints.yml           upstream: analysis/dataset-import-qc/260416
```

- **Run label.** You choose it (e.g. the batch ID, or a setting name such as
  `bmr20`). Several runs of one skill are sibling folders; a run folder is
  never overwritten without asking you.
- **The yml** records every scientific choice of the run: column mapping,
  expected counts, phase windows, BMR settings, exclusions with reasons. The
  agent fills it in with you and never invents a setting.
- **Rendering** is one command in the run folder:

  ```{bash}
  cd analysis/behavior-endpoints/260416
  quarto render behavior-endpoints.qmd --execute-params behavior-endpoints.yml
  ```

- **The manifest** (`outputs/*__manifest.yml`) records the status, the
  parameters, the package version, and every input and output with its md5
  checksum. Status is `complete` (safe to use downstream), `needs_review`
  (stopped for your decision; downstream outputs not written) or `failed`.
- **Upstream.** A run lists the run folders it reads under `upstream:`. A
  skill refuses to start if an upstream run is not `complete`, and warns if
  an upstream output changed after it was written.

## Decisions you make

The skills stop and ask whenever a choice is scientific. The main ones:

| Skill | You decide |
|---|---|
| `dataset-import-qc` | column mapping and types; expected wells and timepoints; which wells to remove (no larva, several larvae, technical failure); plates to exclude |
| `interplate-vc-qc`, `intraplate-vc-qc` | keep or exclude each flagged plate, with a reason |
| `behavior-endpoints` | phase windows (e.g. L1 1-10, D1 11-20, ...); similarity window and metric; plot layout |
| `behavior-endpoints-anova` | significance level; similarity metrics |
| `behavior-endpoints-bmc`, `devtox-endpoints-bmc` | BMR per endpoint type and how it is chosen; direction; per-plate or pooled fitting |

The QC skills do not change the data: they write a list of excluded plates
in their manifest, and the later skills drop those plates when you list the
QC run under `upstream:`.

**Single-larva wells.** After `dataset-import-qc`, every well holds exactly
one larva: `keep_well = TRUE` (analyzed) or `FALSE` (dead or malformed).
Wells with no larva, several larvae or a technical failure are removed
there and only there; later skills never change the wells. See
`?zfbehavior::module1`.

## An example session

> **You:** Import the plates in `data/raw/260416/` with the
> `dataset-import-qc` skill. Run label `260416`.
>
> **Agent:** reads the skill, asks for the plate design (96 wells, 50
> one-minute bins, 16 VC wells and 16 wells per dose) and how problem wells
> are marked, looks at one file, proposes the column mapping and types, and
> waits for your confirmation.
>
> **Agent:** creates `analysis/dataset-import-qc/260416/`, fills in the
> yml, renders. The manifest says `needs_review`: 5 wells have the comment
> "empty" or "2 larvae". You decide to remove them; the agent records this
> in the yml with your reason and renders again: `complete`.
>
> **You:** Now plot the raw responses, then compute the behavioral
> endpoints.

## Without an agent

Every skill can be run by hand: copy the two template files into a new run
folder, fill in the yml following `SKILL.md`, and render. The package
functions can also be used directly in R, as shown in
`vignette("methods", package = "zfbehavior")`; the overview of each
module is at `?zfbehavior::module1` to `?zfbehavior::module5`.
